title: NullPointerException During Primitive Auto-Unboxing
symptoms: NullPointerException thrown on an arithmetic operation or boolean conditional expression.
roast: Opening a gift box that contains literally nothing: Java just collapsed your inventory.
diagnosis: Auto-unboxing implicitly calls .intValue() or .booleanValue() on wrapper classes (Integer, Boolean, etc.). If the wrapper reference is null, a NullPointerException occurs.
debuggingSteps: Check wrapper object nullability before unboxing into primitive
Use primitive types if nullability is not required
Use Optional or Objects.requireNonNullElse / ternary default values
badExample:
Integer count = null;
int total = count + 1; // Throws NullPointerException via count.intValue()
fixedExample:
Integer count = null;
int total = (count != null ? count : 0) + 1;
whyItWorks: Guarding against null before evaluation supplies a fallback primitive value, avoiding the implicit method dispatch on null.
tests: Integer count = null; int total = (count != null ? count : 0) + 1; assert total == 1;

title: ConcurrentModificationException During Collection Iteration
symptoms: ConcurrentModificationException thrown when calling list.remove() inside an enhanced for-loop.
roast: Chopping wood from the tree while standing on the leaves you just broke: gravity says hello.
diagnosis: Enhanced for-loops use an internal Iterator. Modifying the collection directly (e.g. list.remove()) desynchronizes the iterator's modCount and expectedModCount.
debuggingSteps: Use Iterator.remove() explicitly instead of collection.remove()
Use Collection.removeIf(predicate) in modern Java 8+
Collect items to delete in a separate collection, then removeAll
whyItWorks: removeIf updates both the underlying array structure and modCount coherently without iterator desynchronization.
tests: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "", "b")); list.removeIf(String::isEmpty); assert list.size() == 2;

title: Comparing String Values Using '==' Instead of '.equals()'
symptoms: String comparison evaluates to false even though both strings display identical characters.
roast: Looking at two identical dirt blocks and insisting one isn't dirt because they have different entity IDs.
diagnosis: The '==' operator in Java compares object references (memory identity), not lexical contents. Two different String objects with identical characters evaluate to false with '=='.
debuggingSteps: Replace '==' with '.equals()' or Objects.equals(a, b)
Put constant string literal on the left side to prevent NPE: "TARGET".equals(val)
Never rely on the JVM String intern pool for business logic comparisons
whyItWorks: String.equals compares character arrays sequentially, verifying true content equality rather than reference identity.

title: Overriding equals Without Overriding hashCode
symptoms: Objects cannot be retrieved from HashSet or HashMap even though an identical equal object is present.
roast: Hiding your treasure chest in chunk (-5, 12) but searching for it in chunk (10, 4) because your compass is broken.
diagnosis: Hash-based collections use hashCode() to select the storage bucket before checking equals(). If two equal objects have different hashCodes, they land in different buckets and lookups fail.
debuggingSteps: Always override hashCode() whenever overriding equals()
Ensure all fields used in equals() are also factored into hashCode()
Use Objects.hash(field1, field2) for a clean hash computation
whyItWorks: Fulfilling the Object contract guarantees that userA.equals(userB) implies userA.hashCode() == userB.hashCode(), placing them in identical hash buckets.
tests: Set<User> set = new HashSet<>(); User u1 = new User("1"); User u2 = new User("1"); set.add(u1); assert set.contains(u2);

title: File/Stream Resource Leak Omitting try-with-resources
symptoms: Operating system file descriptor exhaustion ('Too many open files') or locked files that cannot be deleted.
roast: Opening 50 Nether portals and leaving every single one active until the lag freezes the universe.
diagnosis: Failing to close streams when exceptions occur leaks OS native file descriptors because standard Garbage Collection does not promptly close underlying file handles.
debuggingSteps: Wrap all AutoCloseable resources in try-with-resources statements
Avoid manual .close() calls in scattered finally blocks
Verify stream chains are safely managed
whyItWorks: try-with-resources guarantees that the resource's close() method is invoked deterministically, even if an exception is thrown.
tests: try (ByteArrayInputStream bais = new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[]{1})) { assert bais.read() == 1; }

title: Integer Object Reference Equality Outside Cache Range [-128, 127]
symptoms: Integer comparison 'a == b' evaluates to true for numbers <= 127, but mysteriously evaluates to false for numbers >= 128.
roast: Stacking 64 blocks works fine, but at block 128 your game decides your blocks are from an alternate dimension.
diagnosis: JVM caches Integer objects in the range -128 to 127 via IntegerCache. Inside this range, autoboxing returns cached instances (so '==' succeeds). Outside, new instances are allocated.
debuggingSteps: Always use .equals() for wrapper objects: a.equals(b)
Or unbox explicitly into primitive int before comparing with '=='
Never rely on JVM reference caching for numeric comparison
whyItWorks: .equals() compares the encapsulated primitive int values rather than reference memory addresses.
tests: Integer a = 200; Integer b = 200; assert a.equals(b);

title: Swallowing Exceptions in Empty Catch Blocks
symptoms: Silent failure: application malfunctions downstream with no stack trace or logs explaining why.
roast: Sweeping exploding TNT under the carpet and pretending nothing made that hissing sound.
diagnosis: Catching an exception without logging or rethrowing swallows critical failure context, leaving the system in an invalid state without diagnostic breadcrumbs.
debuggingSteps: Never leave catch blocks empty or containing just a comment
Log the exception message and full stack trace (logger.error("failed", e))
Rethrow as a domain or runtime exception if recovery is impossible
whyItWorks: Preserving the original exception in the exception chain maintains the stack trace for root-cause diagnosis.
tests: try { throw new IOException("fail"); } catch (IOException e) { assert e.getMessage().equals("fail"); }

title: UnsupportedOperationException When Mutating Arrays.asList()
symptoms: UnsupportedOperationException thrown when calling .add() or .remove() on a list created with Arrays.asList().
roast: Trying to craft armor inside an immutable display pedestal: you can look, but you can't touch.
diagnosis: Arrays.asList() returns a fixed-size private wrapper around the array. Structural modifications (.add, .remove) are not supported and throw UnsupportedOperationException.
debuggingSteps: Wrap Arrays.asList in a mutable new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(...))
Use ArrayList constructor when items need to be added or removed later
Understand the difference between fixed-size, unmodifiable (List.of), and mutable lists
badExample:
List<String> list = Arrays.asList("a", "b");
list.add("c"); // Throws UnsupportedOperationException!
whyItWorks: Instantiating a new java.util.ArrayList provides a fully mutable collection supporting structural add and remove operations.
tests: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("a", "b")); list.add("c"); assert list.size() == 3;

title: Static Method Hiding Mistaken for Virtual Overriding
symptoms: Subclass static method is not called when invoked through a base class reference.
roast: Wearing diamond armor over gold armor and expecting the gold perks to trigger dynamically: static binding doesn't care about your outfit.
diagnosis: Static methods are resolved at compile time based on the reference type, not runtime object type. Static methods cannot be overridden; they are only hidden.
debuggingSteps: Remove 'static' modifier if polymorphic runtime dispatch is needed
Invoke static methods using the class name directly (Parent.show()) rather than object references
Add @Override annotation to catch illegal attempts to override static methods
whyItWorks: Instance methods utilize dynamic method dispatch (vtable) based on the actual runtime object instance.
tests: Parent ref = new Child(); assert ref.getVal() == 2; // with virtual method dispatch

title: NoSuchElementException from Optional.get() Without isPresent()
symptoms: java.util.NoSuchElementException: No value present thrown at runtime.
roast: Opening a lucky block expecting an enchanted golden apple and finding an empty void.
diagnosis: Calling Optional.get() directly without verifying value presence recreates the same vulnerability as NullPointerException. Optional.get() is deprecated in favor of safe alternatives.
debuggingSteps: Replace .get() with .orElse(defaultVal) or .orElseGet(supplier)
Use .orElseThrow(() -> new CustomException(...)) for explicit failure handling
Use functional chaining with .map() and .ifPresent()
badExample:
Optional<String> opt = Optional.empty();
String val = opt.get(); // Throws NoSuchElementException!
fixedExample:
Optional<String> opt = Optional.empty();
String val = opt.orElse("default");
whyItWorks: orElse returns the default value gracefully when the Optional container is empty without throwing exceptions.
